text: New York should expand rent stabilization to cover more apartments.
context: About 1 million NYC apartments are rent-stabilized, limiting how much landlords can raise rents each year. Critics say the system is outdated and discourages building maintenance; supporters argue it's the only thing keeping hundreds of thousands of working-class and middle-income New Yorkers in their homes.

text: The state should override local zoning laws to require more housing near transit hubs.
context: New York suburbs zone most residential land for single-family homes only, blocking denser housing near Metro-North and LIRR stations. Housing advocates and developers say state override is necessary to address a statewide crisis; critics — including many suburban legislators — call it an Albany power grab over local land use.

text: Landlords who leave apartments vacant for over a year should face financial penalties.
context: NYC's 2024 housing survey found over 90,000 apartments vacant but not available for rent — held by owners for renovation, personal use, or speculative purposes. Advocates say a vacancy tax or penalty would pressure landlords to put units back on the market; real estate groups argue many vacancies are temporary and that penalizing owners infringes on private property rights.

text: New York City should build more publicly owned affordable housing rather than relying on private developers.
context: Every major NYC affordable housing program relies on private developers who receive tax breaks and subsidies in exchange for setting aside affordable units — often units that remain out of reach for the lowest-income New Yorkers. Reformers want direct public construction instead; opponents argue government-built housing is slower and more expensive, and point to NYCHA's $40 billion repair backlog as evidence the city can't manage what it already owns.

text: State and local government should ban landlords from refusing tenants because they use housing vouchers.
context: 'Source of income' discrimination — refusing tenants because they use housing vouchers — is banned in NYC but legal in most of New York State. Tenant advocates say a statewide ban is essential; some landlords argue voucher programs come with burdensome inspections and payment delays.

text: New York should accelerate its transition away from natural gas in homes and buildings.
context: NY's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) is one of the most ambitious climate laws in the US, requiring 70% renewable electricity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050. Supporters call it essential for the planet; critics argue the pace is unrealistic and will spike energy bills for working-class households.

text: Offshore wind development should be expanded even if it temporarily raises electricity costs.
context: NY has ambitious offshore wind targets — enough to power 6 million homes by 2035 — but several major projects have been cancelled or delayed due to rising construction costs, supply chain issues, and inflation. Utilities warn the buildout will raise electricity rates in the short term; clean energy advocates say the long-term price stability of wind power outweighs the upfront costs.

text: Addressing climate change should take priority even if it means higher energy costs for households.
context: NY's climate transition is projected to raise electricity and heating costs for households in the short term as the state phases out cheap fossil fuels. Supporters argue the long-term cost of inaction — more intense storms, flooding, and heat waves — far exceeds the upfront investment; critics say low- and middle-income New Yorkers are already struggling with energy bills and can't absorb further increases.

text: Fossil fuel companies should be required to pay into a fund for NY's climate adaptation costs.
context: NY's 2024 Climate Change Superfund Act makes fossil fuel companies financially responsible for climate damage, requiring $75 billion over 25 years to fund flood infrastructure and coastal resilience projects. The amount each company owes is based on their historic emissions. Industry groups warn costs will be passed to consumers through higher gas and heating prices; environmental groups call it long-overdue accountability.

text: New York should ban new natural gas power plant construction.
context: Natural gas supplies about 40% of NY's electricity and serves as backup when wind and solar fall short. The state has blocked some new gas plants under the CLCPA but hasn't enacted a full ban. Clean energy advocates say new gas infrastructure locks in decades of emissions; utilities and grid operators warn that eliminating gas before sufficient renewable capacity exists risks blackouts — particularly during extreme cold snaps when electricity demand spikes.

text: New York should raise income taxes on high earners to fund public services.
context: New York consistently ranks as one of the highest-tax states in the country, with a top state rate of 10.9% plus an additional NYC tax of up to 3.876% for city residents. Proponents say taxing the wealthy is essential to fund public services; opponents argue the rates are already driving high earners and businesses out of state, eroding the tax base everyone depends on.

text: The state should reduce business regulations and taxes to attract more companies and jobs.
context: NY consistently ranks among the worst states for business climate in surveys by groups like the Tax Foundation, citing high taxes, complex regulations, and litigation costs. Supporters of deregulation argue cutting red tape would attract employers and stem the flow of businesses and residents to lower-cost states; critics say these rankings are produced by business lobbies and that NY's strong unions, infrastructure, and talent pool already attract the world's top companies.

text: A small tax on Wall Street financial transactions should fund education and infrastructure.
context: A financial transaction tax (FTT) would place a small fee — typically 0.1% to 0.5% — on stock, bond, and derivatives trades processed in New York. Supporters say it would raise billions from Wall Street to fund schools and transit; opponents warn traders would simply route transactions through other states or countries, costing NY jobs and tax revenue.

text: New York should raise the statewide minimum wage to at least $25 per hour.
context: NYC's minimum wage hit $17/hour in 2024 and is indexed to inflation going forward. Supporters of a higher floor argue $17 is still below a living wage in one of the world's most expensive cities; business groups warn that rapid increases hurt small businesses, restaurants, and nonprofits that can't absorb higher labor costs.

text: New York should create a public bank to fund affordable housing and small business loans.
context: Public bank advocates argue that Wall Street banks systematically underinvest in low-income communities, leaving small businesses and affordable housing developers reliant on predatory lenders or expensive private financing. A state bank could fill that gap; opponents warn it would compete unfairly with private banks, expose the state to financial risk, and become a vehicle for political patronage.

text: New York's bail reform laws should be scaled back to give judges more discretion in setting bail.
context: NY's 2019 bail reform eliminated cash bail for most non-violent crimes, arguing that wealth shouldn't determine who stays in jail before trial. Critics say the changes led to dangerous defendants being released; supporters point to data showing recidivism rates didn't spike and that the old system jailed poor people simply for being poor.

text: The state should significantly increase funding for mental health services as an alternative to arrest.
context: After the 2020 police reform movement, several cities piloted unarmed mental health crisis response units. Supporters argue expanding these programs statewide would reduce unnecessary arrests and hospitalizations, treat root causes of repeated emergency calls, and free up police for violent crime. Opponents contend that many crisis calls involve unpredictable violence, that mental health workers lack the authority or training to de-escalate dangerous situations, and that these programs shouldn't replace police response but supplement it.

text: New York City should increase the size of the NYPD.
context: Crime in New York rose in several categories after 2020, and some communities — particularly in outer boroughs and upstate cities — argue they are underpoliced. Supporters say more officers would deter crime, improve response times, and restore community trust through visibility. Opponents argue that hiring more police is an expensive response that doesn't address root causes like poverty and mental illness, and that the same dollars spent on housing or jobs would produce better long-term safety outcomes.

text: Qualified immunity — which makes it harder to sue police officers — should be eliminated in New York.
context: Qualified immunity is a legal doctrine that shields police officers from personal liability in civil lawsuits unless they violated 'clearly established' law — a high bar that courts rarely find met. Colorado, New Mexico, and NYC have already limited it; supporters of ending it argue it's the only way to hold officers accountable, while police unions say it would expose officers to frivolous lawsuits.

text: New York should close Rikers Island and replace it with smaller, borough-based jails.
context: Rikers holds roughly 6,000 people daily — most awaiting trial, not yet convicted — in conditions that have drawn years of federal scrutiny and inmate deaths. NYC voted in 2019 to close it by 2027 and replace it with smaller borough-based jails; that deadline has since slipped significantly. Reformers say the replacement facilities would be safer and more humane; correction officers' unions and some local communities oppose the borough sites.

text: New York should expand the number of charter schools allowed to operate in the state.
context: NY caps the number of charter schools at 460 statewide, with most slots concentrated in NYC. Supporters of lifting the cap argue charters give low-income families access to better schools outside failing districts; opponents — including teachers unions — say charters drain funding from public schools and lack the same accountability and union protections as traditional public schools.

text: School funding should be equalized so high-poverty districts receive the same per-pupil spending as wealthy ones.
context: NY's Foundation Aid formula was created in 2007 to direct more money to high-need, low-income school districts, but the state underfunded it by billions for over a decade. A court order finally forced full funding in 2024. Supporters say equalized funding is a matter of basic fairness; critics argue money alone doesn't fix failing schools without accountability reforms.

text: Tuition at SUNY and CUNY should be free for all New York State residents.
context: SUNY and CUNY together enroll over 600,000 students and serve as the primary path to higher education for working-class New Yorkers. Supporters argue that free tuition would reduce student debt, increase enrollment among low-income students, and generate long-term economic returns by producing a more educated workforce. Opponents argue the price tag — estimated at over $1.5 billion annually — is too high given the state's existing fiscal pressures, and that the subsidy would largely benefit students who would have attended anyway rather than expanding access to the truly disadvantaged.

text: Parents should have the right to review and formally object to curriculum materials in public schools.
context: Several states have passed parental rights laws giving families the ability to review curriculum and opt children out of certain lessons. Supporters say transparency strengthens the parent-school relationship and ensures local values are reflected in classrooms. Opponents argue these laws are vague enough to be weaponized against any controversial topic, and that curriculum decisions should rest with trained educators and elected school boards — not individual parental veto.

text: New York should eliminate high-stakes standardized tests as a requirement for high school graduation.
context: NY is one of the few states still requiring standardized Regents Exams to graduate high school. Advocates for eliminating them argue the tests are poor predictors of college success, disadvantage students with learning disabilities and English language learners, and push schools to 'teach to the test.' Defenders say they provide a consistent, objective standard that keeps diplomas meaningful.

text: New York should pass the NY Health Act to create a single-payer healthcare system for all state residents.
context: The NY Health Act would create a single state-run health plan covering all NY residents, eliminating premiums, copays, and deductibles. It would be funded by income and payroll taxes, with higher earners paying more. Supporters say it would cover the uninsured and save money by eliminating insurance company overhead; critics warn of massive tax increases, provider flight, and federal legal obstacles.

text: The state should expand Medicaid eligibility to cover more low-income New Yorkers.
context: Medicaid expansion has been shown to reduce uninsured rates, improve health outcomes, and lower uncompensated care costs for hospitals. Supporters argue New York should go further to cover remaining gaps, particularly for undocumented immigrants who are largely excluded. Opponents argue the state's Medicaid program is already strained, that expansions add long-term fiscal obligations, and that federal matching funds don't fully offset state costs.

text: Mental health services should receive funding equal to physical healthcare services in New York.
context: Federal parity law has required equal mental health coverage since 2008, but enforcement has been weak and insurers routinely deny mental health claims at higher rates than medical ones. Supporters of stronger state-level parity requirements argue New York should mandate stricter compliance and real-time audits. Critics say the added mandates raise premiums for all policyholders and that the real problem is a shortage of in-network providers, not coverage rules.

text: New York should negotiate prescription drug prices directly with pharmaceutical companies.
context: New York spends billions annually on prescription drugs through Medicaid and state employee health plans. Supporters argue the state should use that leverage to negotiate directly with manufacturers to lower costs for both government programs and individual consumers. Pharmaceutical companies and some economists counter that price controls reduce investment in new drug development and that federal programs like Medicare negotiation already address this at scale.

text: New York should fund universal pre-K and subsidized childcare for all families statewide.
context: New York City launched universal pre-K in 2014 under Mayor de Blasio, and the state has since expanded the program. Supporters argue extending it statewide — with subsidized childcare — would boost workforce participation, especially for women, and improve early childhood development outcomes. Critics argue the cost is substantial, that quality varies widely across providers, and that means-tested programs targeting the lowest-income families would deliver more value per dollar.

text: New York should maintain sanctuary policies that limit local police cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
context: NY's sanctuary policies restrict local police from doing ICE's job for them — officers generally won't honor ICE detainer requests or share information about immigration status. Advocates say this is essential: immigrant communities are more likely to report crimes when they aren't afraid of deportation. Opponents argue any limit on cooperation with federal law enforcement creates dangerous public safety gaps.

text: The state should provide more funding to shelter and support asylum seekers arriving in New York.
context: NYC spent over $4 billion sheltering and supporting asylum seekers in 2023–2024 — straining the city budget and triggering cuts to other services. The state covered a fraction of those costs. Supporters of more state funding argue NYC bore a disproportionate burden for a national crisis; critics say the city's generous policies attracted more migrants than it could handle.

text: Undocumented immigrants should be eligible for New York State financial aid for college.
context: NY's DREAM Act allows undocumented students who graduated from NY high schools to apply for state financial aid for college. Supporters argue these students grew up in NY, pay taxes, and deserve the same opportunities as their classmates; opponents say state money should be reserved for citizens and legal residents, especially when college costs are rising for everyone.

text: Undocumented immigrants should be allowed to obtain New York driver's licenses.
context: NY's Green Light Law allows undocumented immigrants to obtain standard driver's licenses — one of 19 states to do so. Since passing in 2019, over 250,000 undocumented New Yorkers have obtained licenses, letting them drive legally to work, school, and medical appointments. Supporters say it improves road safety by ensuring all drivers are tested and insured; opponents argue the state shouldn't provide government IDs to people who entered illegally and warn the licenses could be exploited for voter fraud.

text: State and local police in New York should not assist with federal immigration enforcement actions.
context: New York City has been a sanctuary city since the 1980s, with policies limiting cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. Supporters argue these policies encourage immigrant communities to report crimes and cooperate with police without fear of deportation. Critics argue they obstruct federal law, create public safety risks by releasing individuals with criminal records, and that local governments shouldn't nullify federal immigration law.

text: Congestion pricing — tolls on vehicles entering Manhattan below 60th Street — should be kept and expanded.
context: Congestion pricing charges drivers entering Manhattan below 60th Street — most pay $9 per trip — to reduce traffic and fund $15 billion in MTA capital improvements. Early data showed a significant drop in vehicles entering the pricing zone and a reduction in emissions. Opponents argue it unfairly burdens outer-borough commuters and small businesses who have no viable transit alternative.

text: The MTA should receive dedicated, protected state funding that cannot be raided for other purposes.
context: The MTA's capital program has historically been funded through a mix of borrowing, state aid, and federal grants — leaving it vulnerable to budget shortfalls and political interference. Supporters of a dedicated funding stream argue that transit investment requires decades-long planning horizons that annual budget cycles can't support. Critics contend that dedicated streams are inflexible, and that the MTA's chronic cost overruns and governance problems are the real obstacle to modernization.

text: Upstate roads, bridges, and transit should receive state infrastructure investment equal to NYC transit.
context: Upstate advocates have long argued that state infrastructure spending skews heavily toward New York City, leaving roads, bridges, and transit systems in cities like Buffalo, Syracuse, and Rochester chronically underfunded. Supporters of proportional funding say it would correct a structural inequity. Critics argue that population-proportional formulas ignore the disproportionate economic output of the NYC metro area and that needs-based — not per-capita — allocation is the more rational approach.

text: New York City should significantly reduce subway and bus fares or make them free.
context: New York City's subway and bus fares have risen steadily while service quality has remained inconsistent, prompting calls to reduce or eliminate fares entirely. Supporters argue that cheaper transit would increase ridership, cut car traffic, and deliver the largest benefit to low-wage workers who rely on public transit. Opponents contend that fare revenue is essential to MTA operations, and that without a clear replacement — such as a dedicated tax or congestion charge — fare cuts would simply accelerate the agency's debt spiral.

text: New York should invest in high-speed passenger rail connecting NYC, Albany, and Buffalo.
context: The Empire Corridor — connecting New York City, Albany, and Buffalo — is one of the busiest rail corridors in the country, yet trains average under 50 mph due to aging track shared with freight. Supporters of high-speed rail argue that upgrading the corridor would cut travel times dramatically, reduce car and air travel emissions, and boost upstate economies. Critics point to the enormous capital cost, decades-long construction timelines, and the difficulty of building high-speed infrastructure in a densely built Northeast corridor.
